prompt:
Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit.

We represent: defendant issuer.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that generic statements of corporate optimism are inactionable puffery under Section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5.

Cite at least six decisions of the Second Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

Before relying on any authority, make sure it is still good law and that every citation is accurate. Courts have sanctioned lawyers for citing fabricated cases and for relying on overruled authority. Do not cite a case unless you are confident it exists at that citation.

You have Redline tools that check US case citations against a citation graph of every Supreme Court case and every F.3d appeals case. Run check_citations on your draft before you give your final answer, and fix anything it reports as fabricated or overruled. Use search_cases and get_case to look authorities up.
answer:
**ARGUMENT**

**I. The Challenged Statements Are Generic Expressions of Corporate Optimism and Are Inactionable Puffery.**

Section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5 reach only misstatements or omissions of *material* fact. *See Ganino v. Citizens Utils. Co.*, 228 F.3d 154, 161–62 (2d Cir. 2000). A statement is material only if there is a substantial likelihood that a reasonable investor would view it as significantly altering the "total mix" of available information. *Id.* at 162. Under this Circuit's settled law, vague and generalized expressions of corporate optimism cannot meet that standard. They are puffery as a matter of law and can be dismissed under Rule 12(b)(6).

This Circuit has long held that "puffery" is not actionable. Statements that are "too general to cause a reasonable investor to rely upon them" do not alter the total mix of information. *Lasker v. N.Y. State Elec. & Gas Corp.*, 85 F.3d 55, 59 (2d Cir. 1996). Courts have applied this principle repeatedly to general statements of optimism and confidence. *See Rombach v. Chang*, 355 F.3d 164, 174 (2d Cir. 2004). In *Rombach*, the Court held that statements that a company was "well-positioned" for growth, or that its prospects were bright, were "puffery" and "too general." *Id.* The Court has also held that a securities plaintiff cannot rest a fraud claim on "expressions of puffery and corporate optimism." *Novak v. Kasaks*, 216 F.3d 300, 315 (2d Cir. 2000). The Court reasoned that investors and analysts discount such statements because they are not tied to concrete, verifiable facts. *See In re Time Warner Inc. Sec. Litig.*, 9 F.3d 259, 267 (2d Cir. 1993). That reasoning holds even where the optimism later proves unfounded.

The Court has applied the same rule in more recent decisions. In *ECA & Local 134 IBEW Joint Pension Trust v. JP Morgan Chase Co.*, 553 F.3d 187, 206 (2d Cir. 2009), the Court held that generalized statements about a company's risk management, and its commitment to sound practices, were "too general to cause a reasonable investor to rely upon them." The Court therefore held that those statements were not actionable. *Id.* The Court reached the same result in *City of Pontiac Policemen's & Firemen's Retirement System v. UBS AG*, 752 F.3d 173, 183 (2d Cir. 2014). There, generic assertions of a commitment to compliance and integrity were "inactionable puffery." *Id.* It did so again in *IBEW Local Union No. 58 Pension Trust Fund & Annuity Fund v. Royal Bank of Scotland Group, PLC*, 783 F.3d 383, 390 (2d Cir. 2015). There, the Court held that broad statements about a company's strength and its risk controls were not actionable. *Id.* And in *Singh v. Cigna Corp.*, 918 F.3d 57, 63 (2d Cir. 2019), the Court reaffirmed that general statements about compliance and business practices are non-actionable puffery. It found that no reasonable investor would rely on them as guarantees of specific facts. *Id.*

These precedents control here. The statements the plaintiffs challenge are the kind this Circuit has repeatedly held inactionable. They include statements that the Company was "well positioned," had "confidence" in its strategy, and expected "continued strong performance." None of them asserts a specific, verifiable fact. None gives a concrete metric, a guarantee, or a representation about a particular present condition. A reasonable investor would read them as the ordinary language of management optimism. Such an investor would look to the Company's concrete financial disclosures for facts. *See Time Warner*, 9 F.3d at 267; *Rombach*, 355 F.3d at 174.

The plaintiffs cannot avoid this rule by pointing to later adverse developments. Hindsight does not convert optimistic opinion into a misrepresentation of fact. *See Novak*, 216 F.3d at 315. The question is whether the statement, when made, was specific enough that a reasonable investor would have relied on it. *See Lasker*, 85 F.3d at 59. Because these statements were not, they are immaterial as a matter of law. The Section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5 claims premised on them should be dismissed.
